slides.title: Rui's school day
text: Rui is eleven and he lives in Setúbal. On school days he wakes up at quarter past seven. He has a shower, gets dressed and has breakfast with his dad: toast and a glass of milk.

He goes to school on foot at eight o'clock. He has lunch in the school canteen at one o'clock. In the afternoon he has PE, his favourite subject. At home, he does his homework and plays with his dog, Bolinha. He goes to bed at half past nine.

story.title: The Fox and the Sleeping Clock
story.subtitle: A school year full of clues
story.blurb: The clock on the school tower always says a quarter past four. On his first day in Lisbon, Oliver finds a card in his desk with a drawing of a fox and a message: "I know your secret." Who is The Fox, and how does The Fox know so much?

chapters.title: A Card in the Desk
paragraphs: It is the fifteenth of September, the first day of school, and Inês Matos is late. Inês is ten years old, and she is a detective. Detectives are never late.

She runs up the hill with her red notebook in her hand. Her school is old and yellow, with a tall white tower. At the top of the tower there is a clock. Its hands say a quarter past four. They always say a quarter past four. The clock is asleep, and nobody can wake it up.
Senhor Bento, the caretaker, is at the gate. He is tall and grey, with a long moustache and a big bunch of keys on his belt. He looks at his watch. Then he looks at Inês. He never smiles.
"Inês! Over here!"
It is Tiago Rocha, her best friend. Tiago is eleven. He has got curly black hair, a big smile and a sandwich in his hand. There is always a sandwich in Tiago's hand.
"Are you hungry? It's half past eight in the morning!" says Inês.
"I'm not hungry," says Tiago. "I'm nervous. When I'm nervous, I eat."

Their classroom is on the first floor. It has got big windows, twenty-four desks and a map of the world on the wall. On every desk there is a small card with a name. Behind them there is a new name: Oliver Brown.
"Oliver Brown?" says Tiago. "Who's he?"
The door opens and a boy comes in. He is thin and quiet. He has got red hair, round glasses and a blue backpack.
"Hi! Are you Oliver?" asks Inês. "I'm Inês, and this is Tiago."

"Hello. Yes, I'm Oliver," says the boy. "I'm from Manchester, in England. My dad is English and my mum is Portuguese. We live here now." His Portuguese is good, but his accent is funny, and Tiago laughs. Oliver's face goes red.
"Sorry, sorry!" says Tiago. "Your Portuguese is great. My English is terrible. Listen: Hello, my name are Tiago."
"Is," says Oliver. "My name is Tiago." And for the first time, he smiles.
The English teacher is new too. She is young and tall, with short blond hair, a long green scarf and a green pen behind her ear.

"Good morning, everyone! I'm Miss Hart, and I'm from Edinburgh, in Scotland." She takes the pen from behind her ear. "And this is my magic pen. I mark all your homework with it. Red is a scary colour. Green is a friendly colour."
"I like her," whispers Tiago. "She's funny."

At one o'clock the canteen is hot and noisy. Dona Amélia is behind the counter with a very big spoon. She is small and old, with white hair and round glasses, and she sings when she works. Today her song is in English.
She looks at Oliver. Then she puts an extra potato on his plate. "There you go, love," she says. Her English is perfect.
"Thank you!" says Oliver, surprised.
"Dona Amélia speaks English?" asks Inês.
"Dona Amélia speaks everything," says Tiago. "She speaks soup. She speaks rice. She speaks chocolate pudding."
After lunch, Oliver opens his desk to put his books inside. Then he stops.
Inside the desk there is a small white card. On the card there is a drawing of an orange fox, and a message in green ink:
"Welcome, Oliver Brown. You are new here, and I am very old. The clock in the tower is asleep. Can you and your friends wake it up? I know your secret. Your first clue is at home. The Fox"
Inês looks at the green ink. Then she looks at Miss Hart's green pen. She opens her red notebook and writes: Suspect number one.
"Who is The Fox?" asks Tiago.
"I don't know," says Oliver. "I'm new. Nobody knows me here."
"And what is your secret?" asks Inês.
"I haven't got a secret," says Oliver. But his ears are red, very red, and Inês is a detective. She knows a lie when she sees one.
"Your first clue is at home," she reads slowly. "But Oliver, it's a new house for you. How has The Fox got a clue in your house?"

chapters.title: The Third Stair
paragraphs: For six weeks, Oliver looks for the clue in his house every day. He looks in the kitchen and in the bathroom. He looks under his bed and inside his wardrobe. He finds two buttons, a spider and a very old biscuit. He doesn't find a clue.
"You need a detective," says Inês. "You need me."

So on the thirty-first of October, Halloween, Inês and Tiago are at Oliver's house. Tiago's dog is with them. Her name is Bolacha. She is fat, brown and very lazy, and tonight she is a pumpkin. Tiago's mum makes her costume. Bolacha hates it.

Oliver's house is old and tall, with blue and white tiles on the walls. Downstairs it has got a kitchen, a living room and a small garden with a lemon tree. Upstairs it has got three bedrooms and a bathroom.

Oliver's dad is in the kitchen. He has got a big orange pumpkin and a knife. "This is a jack-o'-lantern," he says. "In England we put a candle inside it on Halloween. Children wear scary costumes and go from door to door. They say 'Trick or treat!' and the neighbours give them sweets."
"We've got something like that in Portugal," says Inês. "It's called Pão-por-Deus, and it's on the first of November. Children knock on doors and ask for bread, cakes and sweets."
"Bread?" says Tiago. "I want sweets." He is a vampire tonight, with a black cape and plastic teeth.

Inês is a detective, of course. She has got a brown hat and her grandpa's magnifying glass. Oliver is a skeleton. His mum looks at the three of them and laughs. "Your costumes are great. Is that dog a pumpkin?"
"She's a pumpkin," says Tiago. "She isn't happy about it."
Inês opens her notebook. "Oliver, whose house is this? Is it your parents' house?"
"No, it isn't ours," says Oliver. "It's an old lady's house. Mum says she's very kind. She lives in a flat over the bakery, but I never see her."
Inês writes: Old lady. Bakery. Then she looks at Oliver. "And now, your secret. Detectives need all the information."
Oliver looks at the floor. Then he goes to his bedroom and comes back with a small tin. Inside there are some coins and two notes.

"This is my secret," he says quietly. "It's my money for a plane ticket. I want to go back to Manchester. My grandma is there. My friends are there. My football team is there. Here, everything is different."
"How much money have you got?" asks Tiago.
"Forty-two euros."
Tiago opens his mouth, but Inês kicks his foot. A plane ticket is more than forty-two euros, and everyone knows it.
"OK," says Inês. "Your secret is safe with us. Now let's find that clue."
They look everywhere. They look behind the sofa, under the armchair and inside the old wardrobe in the hall. Nothing.
Then Tiago goes up the stairs. On the third stair there is a noise. It is a hollow noise, like a drum.
"Again!" says Inês. Tiago jumps on the third stair. Bom. Bom. Bom.
"It's empty," says Inês. "There's something under it."

The board on the third stair is loose. Oliver pulls it, and it opens like a little door. Under it there is an old metal box. Inside the box there are two things: an old black and white photo and a sheet of paper.

The photo shows a girl with long plaits. She is in front of their school, under the tower. The girl isn't happy. On the back of the photo there are some words in green ink: "This is me. I am ten here. Remember, remember the fifth of November."
The paper is blank. Inês puts it near her nose. "It smells of lemons," she says.
Then, suddenly, the lights go out. The house is dark. Bolacha barks.
"Look!" whispers Oliver. He points at the window.
In the garden, under the lemon tree, there is a person with a torch. The torch moves up, and they can see the face. It is orange, with long ears and a black nose.
It is the face of a fox.

chapters.title: Remember, Remember
paragraphs: Oliver's dad runs into the garden with the light of his phone. Inês, Tiago and Oliver run behind him. Bolacha stays on the sofa. She is a pumpkin, not a hero.
The garden is empty. The gate is open. The fox is gone.
But under the lemon tree there is something on the grass. Inês picks it up with a tissue, because detectives never touch evidence with their fingers. It is a pen. A green pen.
"Miss Hart's magic pen!" says Tiago.
"Maybe," says Inês. "There are a lot of green pens in Lisbon." But she puts the pen in a plastic bag, and she writes in her notebook: Suspect number one has got a fox mask?
Five days later, on the fifth of November, Inês and Tiago are at Oliver's house again. It is cold and dark. In the garden, Oliver's dad has got a small fire in a metal bowl.

"Tonight is Bonfire Night," he says. "In 1605, a man called Guy Fawkes and his friends have got a plan. They want to blow up the Houses of Parliament in London, with the King inside. But the plan fails. Now, every year on the fifth of November, people in Britain light bonfires and watch fireworks. And children say a poem: 'Remember, remember the fifth of November.'"
"Remember, remember!" says Oliver. "Like the words on the photo!"
Inês takes the blank paper out of her bag. "Mr Brown, lemon juice is an invisible ink. When the paper is hot, the words appear. Can you help us?"
"Fire isn't for children," says Oliver's dad. "But I can do it." He holds the paper over the bowl, high and very carefully. Slowly, brown letters appear, one by one:
"The sleeping clock has got three keys. Key number one is on a tree, in a big room, on a happy day. The Fox"
"A tree?" says Tiago. "There are a million trees in Lisbon!"
"On a happy day," says Oliver. "What is a happy day with a tree?"
Inês closes her notebook. "Christmas," she says.

In December, the school hall has got a huge Christmas tree. It has got lights, stars, two gold angels and about a hundred red balls. There are presents under it, but they are empty boxes. Tiago knows. He checks every box.
On the last day of term there is a Christmas party in the hall. Miss Hart is in a red jumper with a reindeer on it. She has got a plate of mince pies.

"In Britain we eat these at Christmas," she says. "And on the twenty-fifth of December we have a big lunch with turkey, potatoes and Christmas pudding. At night, Father Christmas comes down the chimney and puts presents in the children's stockings."
"In Portugal the big dinner is on the twenty-fourth," says Inês. "It's called Consoada. We eat bacalhau with potatoes and cabbage, and then bolo-rei."
"Bolo-rei is the king of cakes," says Tiago. He has got a mince pie in each hand.
Inês takes the green pen out of her bag. "Miss Hart, is this your pen?"
"My magic pen! Thank you, Inês!" Miss Hart puts it behind her ear. "I lose a pen every week. They are always in strange places."
She doesn't look like a fox. But foxes are clever, thinks Inês.

Then she walks round the tree, very slowly. She looks at the stars, the angels, the lights and the balls. The balls are all the same. No, they aren't. One ball has got a thin line in the middle. Inês turns it, and it opens like an egg.
Inside there is a key. It is small, old and golden, and it has got a tiny label: 1/3.
"Key number one!" whispers Oliver.
Tiago forgets his mince pies. Inês holds the key in her hand. It is cold and heavy, and her heart is fast.
Then a big hand closes on Inês's shoulder. She turns round. It is Senhor Bento. His keys go clink, clink on his belt. He looks at the little golden key in her hand, and his face is white.
"Where is that from?" he says. "Give it to me, menina. Now."

chapters.title: A Quarter Past Four
paragraphs: Inês closes her hand. Her heart is very loud. "It's... it's my Christmas present," she says. "From my grandma."
Senhor Bento looks at her for a long time. Then he looks up at the tower. "That tower is dangerous," he says quietly. "Remember that." And he walks away. Clink, clink, clink.
"He knows about the key," says Oliver.
"He knows about the clock," says Tiago.
"And he never smiles," says Inês. She opens her notebook and writes: Suspect number two.
In January, Inês has got a plan. "Detectives watch people," she says. "We can watch Senhor Bento. Every day. Every hour."
"I can't watch him every hour," says Tiago. "I've got maths, I've got football and I've got lunch."
So they share the work, and after two weeks there is a new page in the red notebook: The Routine of Senhor Bento.

He arrives at school at half past seven. He opens the gate at eight o'clock. At half past ten he drinks a coffee in the kitchen with Dona Amélia. At one o'clock he has lunch in the canteen. And at a quarter past four, every day, he stands under the tower and looks up at the clock. He looks at it for five minutes. He never says a word.
"That's strange," says Oliver. "Why at a quarter past four?"
"Because the clock always says a quarter past four," says Inês. "Maybe it's his favourite time."

Their own routines are not so interesting. Inês gets up at seven o'clock. She has breakfast, brushes her teeth and walks to school with her mum. Oliver gets up at half past six, because he can't sleep. He thinks about Manchester, and his grandma, and the rain.
Tiago gets up at five to eight. Every day. He puts on his clothes in two minutes, eats his toast in the street and arrives at school at twenty-nine minutes past eight. He is very proud of this.
There are no new clues in January. There is no fox. There is only rain, cold hands and a maths test on a Monday morning.

Then, one Wednesday, there is fish soup for lunch. Tiago doesn't like fish soup, but he eats it. Oliver lifts his bowl and stops. Under the bowl there is a paper napkin, and on the napkin there are some words in green ink:
"Well done, detectives. Key number two is in a room with a thousand books. Look for the red dragon. The Fox"
"A room with a thousand books... the library!" says Tiago.
"A red dragon," says Oliver slowly. "There's a red dragon on the flag of Wales. Wales is a country in the UK, next to England."

"But who puts a napkin under your bowl?" asks Inês. She looks round the canteen. There are two hundred children, ten teachers and a lot of noise. Dona Amélia is behind the counter with her big spoon. She is singing again. Miss Hart is at the teachers' table, with her green pen behind her ear. And Senhor Bento is at a small table near the door, with a bowl of soup in front of him.
Inês checks her notebook. One o'clock: Senhor Bento has lunch in the canteen. Correct.
Then she looks out of the window, at the tower, and she can't breathe.
The clock moves. The big hand goes from a quarter past four to twenty past four. Then to twenty-five past four. Then to half past four.
"Oliver! Tiago! Look!"
There is a face in the little window under the clock. It is a man's face, with a long white beard. He looks down at the school for a second. Then the face is gone.
Inês looks at the canteen again. Senhor Bento is here. Miss Hart is here. Dona Amélia is here.
So who is in the tower?

chapters.title: The Red Dragon
paragraphs: Nobody believes them. "The clock? It always says a quarter past four," says Miss Hart. "Look." And she is right. In the afternoon the hands say a quarter past four again, like always.
"Someone moves them back," says Inês. "Someone with a key."

But first they need key number two. The school library is on the second floor, next to the music room. It is small and quiet, and it smells of old paper. There are books on the shelves, books on the tables, books on the floor and books under the chairs.
"There aren't a thousand books here," says Tiago. "There are a million."

They can only go to the library at lunchtime, and lunchtime is short. So for two weeks they eat fast and search fast. Every detective in the team has got a special talent. Inês can find things. Oliver can read English very fast, and he can draw anything. Tiago can't read fast, but he can climb, and he can make the librarian laugh. That is important too.
"Is this a dragon?" asks Oliver. He has got a big green book in his hands.
"That's a dinosaur," says Inês. "And those books over there are about cooking. Look at these, on the bottom shelf. These are about animals."
Tiago opens a book about dogs. "This dog looks like Bolacha. Have you got a pet, Oliver?"
"Not here," says Oliver. "I've got a cat in Manchester. She lives with my grandma now. Her name is Biscuit."
Tiago stares at him. "Biscuit? Bolacha means biscuit! Our pets have got the same name. They're twins!"
"Shhh!" says the librarian. But she is smiling.

On the fourteenth of February there is a pink envelope on Tiago's desk. Inside there is a card with a big red heart and a poem: "Roses are red, violets are blue, your dog is lazy, but I love you. Guess who?"
The writing is green.
"Green ink!" says Tiago. His face is redder than the heart. "Miss Hart loves me!"
"Miss Hart writes everything in green," says Inês. "Our homework is green. Our tests are green."
"In England, people often send Valentine cards with no name," says Oliver. "It's a tradition. That's the fun."
Tiago puts the card in his pocket. All day he smiles at everyone, just in case.

Then, on a rainy Friday, Tiago climbs the library ladder. On the top shelf, between a big atlas and a book about cats, there is a red book. On its cover there is a dragon. The title is Wales: The Land of the Red Dragon.
"This one!" says Tiago. "It's very heavy."

He gives it to Inês. She opens it on the table. In the middle of the book there is a square hole in the pages, like a little box. And in the box there is a small golden key with a label: 2/3. Under the key there is a card with a fox on it.
"Key number three is in the capital of Scotland. The Fox"
"The capital of Scotland is Edinburgh," says Oliver.
"And who is from Edinburgh?" asks Inês.
They look at each other. "Miss Hart."
That night, Inês puts the two keys in her pencil case. She puts her pencil case in her schoolbag, and her schoolbag under her bed. She sleeps with one eye open.

In the morning she carries her bag to school. At break she leaves it in the classroom, under her desk, like every day. The door is locked. Only the teachers and Senhor Bento have got keys to that door.
After break, Inês sits down and opens her pencil case. Her pencils are there. Her rubber is there. Her ruler is there.
The keys are not there.
In their place there is a small piece of paper. The words are not green. They are black, in big capital letters:
"THE TOWER IS NOT A GAME. STOP NOW."

chapters.title: Red, White and Blue
paragraphs: "Who can open our classroom at break?" asks Inês. She writes the answer in her notebook: The teachers. Senhor Bento.
"Or Miss Hart," says Tiago sadly. "My Valentine."
"Your Valentine is maybe a thief," says Inês. "Or a fox. Or both."
In March, Miss Hart has got a big project: UK Day. On that day everyone wears red, white and blue, the colours of the British flag.

Inês is in a red jumper, a white skirt and blue trainers. Oliver is in his red Manchester United shirt, white trousers and a blue jacket. Tiago is in a blue tracksuit, red socks and a tall white chef's hat.
"A chef's hat?" says Inês.
"It's white," says Tiago. "It counts."
Miss Hart is in a tartan skirt, green and blue, like a Scottish kilt. There are little flags on the walls and a big map of the UK on the board.

Oliver stands in front of the class with a big flag. His hands shake a little, but his voice is clear. "This is the Union Jack. It has got three crosses. The red cross is the cross of St George, for England. The white cross on the blue is the cross of St Andrew, for Scotland. And the red cross like an X is the cross of St Patrick, for Ireland."
"And Wales?" asks a girl.
"Wales isn't on the flag," says Oliver. "That's why the Welsh people love their red dragon so much."

Then Inês points at the map. "The UK has got four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The capital of England is London. The capital of Scotland is Edinburgh. The capital of Wales is Cardiff, and the capital of Northern Ireland is Belfast."
"And the King?" asks Tiago. "Where is he?"
"The King of the United Kingdom is Charles the Third," says Miss Hart. "One of his homes is Buckingham Palace, in London."
"Has he got a dog?" asks Tiago.
"Focus, Tiago," whispers Inês.

At eleven o'clock, the head teacher, Professora Graça, comes into the classroom. "Children, I have got news. Our school is ninety-nine years old. On the first of June, Children's Day, it is one hundred! There is a big party in the playground. And I've got a dream. I want that old clock to wake up for the party. But nobody has got the keys. Nobody knows where they are."
"We know," whispers Tiago. "Well, we know a little."
At lunchtime the classroom is empty. The three detectives stand in front of the big map.
"This is Miss Hart's classroom," says Inês quietly. "That is her map, and those are her pens. The capital of Scotland is here." She puts her finger on Edinburgh.
Inês and Oliver hold the chair. Tiago climbs up and looks behind the map, just behind Edinburgh. There is a piece of tape, and under the tape there is a small golden key with a label: 3/3.
"Number three!" says Tiago.
"One key in our hands, two keys with a thief," says Oliver. "Who has got them?"
That afternoon, at ten past four, they hide behind the big bins near the tower. It is cold and the bins smell of old bananas.

At a quarter past four, Senhor Bento comes out of the school, like every day. He stands under the tower and looks up at the clock. Then he takes the big bunch of keys from his belt. There are big keys, small keys, old keys and new keys.
And between them, two little golden keys shine in the sun. They have got two tiny labels: 1 and 2.
"Oh no," whispers Oliver.
Inês's notebook falls from her hand. It lands on the ground with a loud slap.
Senhor Bento turns round. He looks straight at the bins.
"Who's there?"

chapters.title: Eggs and Answers
paragraphs: Nobody moves. Nobody breathes. Senhor Bento takes a step towards the bins.
Then a grey cat jumps out from behind them and runs across the playground.
"Just a cat," says Senhor Bento, and he goes back inside. Clink, clink, clink. Behind the bins, three detectives breathe again.

The next day, they sit at their usual table in the canteen. It is the last week before the Easter holidays. Tiago always eats everything: soup, rice, chicken, salad and two desserts. One of the desserts is usually Inês's. Inês never eats fish, and she hardly ever eats salad. Oliver sometimes misses his food from home.
"In Manchester I often have beans on toast," he says.
"Beans? On toast?" says Tiago. "For lunch?"
"It's delicious. And here you eat bacalhau every week."
"My grandpa says there are three hundred and sixty-five ways to cook bacalhau," says Inês. "One for every day of the year."
Dona Amélia walks past their table and puts an extra chocolate pudding in front of Tiago. "You always look hungry, my boy," she says.
But Inês isn't hungry. "We need to talk to Senhor Bento," she says. "Today."
"Talk to him?" says Tiago. "He never talks. He hardly ever says good morning."

That afternoon, Miss Hart has got a surprise: an Easter egg hunt in the school garden. "In Britain, children often look for chocolate eggs in the garden at Easter," she says. "We usually eat hot cross buns too. They are sweet buns with a cross on top."
"In Portugal we eat folar and amêndoas," says Inês. "And godparents usually give a folar to their godchildren. My godmother always gives me one."
The children run everywhere. Tiago finds seven eggs. He eats four. Inês finds three. And Oliver finds a blue egg under a bush, with a name on it in green ink: OLIVER.
He opens it. There is no chocolate inside. There is a small piece of paper.
"Don't be angry with the man with the keys. He is a good man and he is always careful. See you at the top of the tower on the first of June, at twelve o'clock. The Fox"
"The Fox knows about the keys," says Oliver.
"The Fox knows everything," says Tiago, with chocolate on his chin.

At a quarter past four, the three of them walk to the tower. Senhor Bento is there, like every day. Tiago's legs shake. Oliver holds the blue egg very tightly. Inês opens her notebook, just to have something in her hands.
"Senhor Bento," she says. "You've got our keys."
Senhor Bento looks at them for a long time. Then he sits down on the steps of the tower, and he does something very strange. He smiles.

"Yes," he says. "I've got your keys. Listen to me. The stairs in that tower are very old, and some of them are broken. Children never go up there. Never. On Wednesdays, a friend of mine goes up. His name is Senhor Fonseca. He is a clockmaker, and he repairs the stairs and the clock."
"A man with a white beard?" asks Oliver.
"That's him. In May the stairs are safe, and I give you the keys. I promise."
"So you are The Fox!" says Tiago.
Senhor Bento laughs. It is a strange, rusty laugh, like an old door. "Me? No, no, no. I'm not clever enough to be The Fox."
"Then who is The Fox?" asks Inês.
Senhor Bento stands up, and his keys go clink, clink. He looks up at the clock. It says a quarter past four, like always.
"The Fox," he says, "is my big sister."
And he walks away before they can say another word.

chapters.title: Questions, Questions
paragraphs: "His big sister?" says Tiago, for the hundredth time. "Who is Senhor Bento's big sister?"
Inês opens her red notebook on a new page. At the top she writes QUESTIONS, in capital letters.
Who is she? How old is she? Where does she live? Why does she write in English? How does she know Oliver's secret? Why does she want the clock to wake up?

"We know some answers," says Inês. "She is old, because her first card says 'I am very old'. She speaks English. She can go into Oliver's house, and she can go into our school. And she is the girl in the old photo."
Oliver takes the photo out of his pocket. He always carries it now. The girl with the plaits looks at them with sad eyes.
In May, Miss Hart has got another surprise. "Today we've got a video call with a school in England," she says. "Oliver's old school, in Manchester!"
Oliver's face goes pink. On the big screen there are twenty-six children in grey jumpers and blue ties. They wave and shout, "Hi, Ollie!"
Miss Hart writes on the board: Ask questions! Use What, Where, When, Who and Why.
"Why do you wear a uniform?" asks Inês.
"Everyone wears one at our school," says a girl called Amy. "Most schools in England have got a uniform. We wear it every day."
"What do you have for lunch?" asks Tiago. Of course.
"Some of us have school dinners, and some of us bring a packed lunch from home," says a boy called Jack. "Sandwiches, crisps and an apple."
"Only a sandwich?" says Tiago. "Here we've got soup, a main dish and a dessert. Every day!"
The English children look at each other. "Soup? Every day?"
Then Jack looks at Oliver. "Do you want to come back, Ollie? We miss you."
Oliver looks at the screen. Then he looks at Inês and Tiago. "I... I don't know," he says.

That evening, Inês walks home past the bakery. Next to the bakery door there is a small green door with a doorbell. There is a name on the doorbell. Inês reads it. She stops. She reads it again, and her eyes go very big.
She opens her notebook, writes one word and closes it fast.
"What is it?" asks Tiago the next day. "Who is she? Tell me!"
"Not yet," says Inês. "A detective needs to be sure."
At the end of May, Senhor Bento comes to the classroom door. He doesn't say good morning. He says, "The stairs are ready."
The first of June is a sunny day. It is Children's Day and the school's hundredth birthday. There are balloons in the playground, a band, a huge cake and two hundred children in their best clothes.
At a quarter to twelve, Senhor Bento takes the three detectives to the tower. He gives them the two golden keys, and Inês takes the third key out of her pocket.

"Listen carefully," he says. "Open this door with key number one. Go up slowly. Hold the rail. Don't run. Don't touch the old bell. Open the door at the top with key number two. And key number three... The Fox knows."
"Aren't you coming with us?" asks Oliver.
"No. This is your adventure, not mine."

Key number one turns with a loud click. The door opens. Inside the tower it is dark and cool, and it smells of dust. They go up, and up, and up. Tiago counts the stairs. "Eighty-five, eighty-six, eighty-seven..."
At the top there is a small wooden door. Inês puts key number two in the lock. Her hand shakes. She turns it.
The door opens. The clock room is full of light. There are big metal wheels, an old bell and a little window over the playground.
In the middle of the room, on an old chair, there is a person in a long grey coat, with a cup of tea. The person has got an orange face, long ears and a black nose.
"Hello, detectives," says The Fox. "You're late."

chapters.title: Twelve O'Clock
paragraphs: The Fox puts down the cup of tea. Then, slowly, The Fox takes off the mask.
White hair. Round glasses. A smile they know very well.
"Dona Amélia?" says Tiago. "But... but you're the soup lady!"
"I'm the soup lady," says Dona Amélia, "and I'm The Fox. A woman can do two things, you know."
Inês isn't surprised. She opens her notebook and shows them the word: RAPOSO. "Amélia Raposo. It's the name on your doorbell, next to the bakery. Raposo, raposa. Fox!"
He takes the old photo out of his pocket. He looks at the girl with the plaits. Then he looks at Dona Amélia. They have got the same eyes.
"It's you," he says.

"It's me. In that photo I'm ten years old, and I'm new at this school. My mother is English, from London, and my father is Portuguese. I speak English at home and bad Portuguese at school. The children laugh at my accent. I haven't got any friends. Every night I want to go back to London." She looks at Oliver. "Does that sound familiar?"
Oliver nods.

"Then one day there is a card in my desk, with a drawing of a fox. It's from my teacher. Every month there is a new clue, and I can't find the clues alone. So I ask a girl for help, and then a boy. At the end of the year I've got two best friends."
"And our house?" asks Oliver.
"The house with the blue tiles is my old home. Your mum is my friend. We have tea together every Sunday. A mother always knows when her son is sad, Oliver. And she tells me."
Oliver's ears go red. "So that's how you know my secret."
"What about the green pen?" asks Inês.
Dona Amélia laughs. "Miss Hart forgets a pen in the canteen every week. I've got a box of them. Green ink for a fox? Perfect."
"And the fox in the garden on Halloween?"
"Me, of course. I want to see your faces when you find my box. An old fox is a curious fox. But the lights aren't me. That house has got very old electricity."
"And Senhor Bento? Why a quarter past four?"
"When we are children, school finishes at a quarter past four, and every day Bento and I meet under this tower. My little brother is a romantic."
"And the Valentine card?" asks Tiago, very quietly.
Dona Amélia winks. "You always eat all your soup, Tiago. I like that in a boy." Tiago's face goes as red as a tomato.
"Now, detectives. It's two minutes to twelve. Senhor Fonseca sets the hands this morning, but the clock is still asleep. Where is key number three?"
Inês gives it to Oliver. Dona Amélia shows him a small hole in the side of the clock. "Put the key in here. Turn it ten times. Slowly."
Oliver turns the key. One, two, three. Inês turns it too. Four, five, six. Then Tiago. Seven, eight, nine, ten.
For a second, nothing happens. Then there is a click. Then a tick. Then a tock. The big metal wheels begin to move. The big hand climbs to the top of the clock.
BONG.

The old bell rings over the school. Twelve times. Down in the playground, two hundred children shout and cheer. Miss Hart waves her long green scarf. And under the tower, Senhor Bento smiles a big, big smile.
"Inês, Tiago," says Oliver. "I've got something to tell you. About my money."
"I don't want a plane ticket now. Well, maybe in August, for a visit to Grandma and Biscuit. But then I come back. Here."
"And the forty-two euros?" asks Tiago.
Oliver smiles. "Pastéis de nata. For everyone in this tower."
"Forty-two euros of pastéis de nata?" says Tiago. "This is the best day of my life."
Dona Amélia gives Inês a small white card with a drawing of a fox. "For September," she says. "Every year there is a new boy or a new girl. And a fox always needs good detectives."
Above them, the clock says twelve o'clock. And for the first time in many, many years, it is right.

reading.title: A Card in the Desk
text: It is the first day of school in Lisbon. Inês Matos is ten years old and she is a detective. She has got a red notebook. Her school is old and yellow, with a tall white tower. At the top of the tower there is a clock. It always says a quarter past four.
Tiago Rocha is Inês's best friend. He is eleven. He has got curly black hair and a big smile, and he is always hungry.
There is a new boy in the class. His name is Oliver Brown. He is from Manchester, in England. He has got red hair and round glasses. His dad is English and his mum is Portuguese.

The new English teacher is Miss Hart. She is from Edinburgh, in Scotland. She has got short blond hair and a green pen. At lunch, Dona Amélia, the canteen lady, gives Oliver an extra potato. Her English is perfect.

After lunch, Oliver opens his desk. Inside there is a small white card with a drawing of an orange fox. The message is in green ink: "Welcome, Oliver Brown. The clock in the tower is asleep. Can you and your friends wake it up? I know your secret. Your first clue is at home. The Fox"
"Who is The Fox?" asks Tiago. Nobody knows. "And what is your secret?" asks Inês. "I haven't got a secret," says Oliver. But his ears are very red.

reading.title: The Third Stair
text: It is the thirty-first of October, Halloween. Inês and Tiago are at Oliver's house. Tiago's dog, Bolacha, is with them. She is fat and lazy, and tonight she is a pumpkin.
Oliver's house is old and tall, with blue and white tiles. Downstairs it has got a kitchen, a living room and a small garden with a lemon tree. Upstairs it has got three bedrooms and a bathroom.

Oliver's dad makes a jack-o'-lantern. "In England, children say 'Trick or treat!' and the neighbours give them sweets," he says. "In Portugal we've got Pão-por-Deus on the first of November," says Inês.
The house isn't Oliver's. It is an old lady's house. She lives in a flat over the bakery.
Then Oliver tells his friends his secret. He has got forty-two euros in a tin. It is his money for a plane ticket, because he wants to go back to Manchester.

The friends look for the clue everywhere. Then Tiago jumps on the third stair. It is hollow! Under it there is an old metal box with an old photo of a girl and a blank sheet of paper. The paper smells of lemons.
Suddenly the lights go out. In the garden, under the lemon tree, there is a person with a torch. The person has got the face of a fox.

reading.title: Remember, Remember
text: On Halloween night, the fox in the garden runs away. Under the lemon tree, Inês finds a green pen. Is it Miss Hart's pen?

On the fifth of November, Oliver's dad has got a small fire in a metal bowl. "Tonight is Bonfire Night," he says. "In 1605, Guy Fawkes and his friends want to blow up the Houses of Parliament in London. But the plan fails. Now, every year, people in Britain light bonfires and watch fireworks."

Inês has got an idea. The blank paper smells of lemons, and lemon juice is an invisible ink. Mr Brown holds the paper over the fire. Brown letters appear: "The sleeping clock has got three keys. Key number one is on a tree, in a big room, on a happy day."
A tree on a happy day? Christmas! In December the school hall has got a huge Christmas tree with lights, stars, two angels and about a hundred red balls.

At the Christmas party, Miss Hart has got a plate of mince pies. "In Britain, Father Christmas comes down the chimney and puts presents in the children's stockings," she says. "In Portugal the big dinner is on the twenty-fourth. It's called Consoada," says Inês.
One red ball on the tree opens like an egg. Inside there is an old golden key! But then Senhor Bento, the caretaker, puts his big hand on Inês's shoulder. "Give it to me. Now."

reading.title: A Quarter Past Four
text: Senhor Bento doesn't take the key. "That tower is dangerous," he says, and he walks away. Inês writes in her notebook: Suspect number two.

In January the three friends watch Senhor Bento every day. He arrives at school at half past seven. He opens the gate at eight o'clock. At half past ten he drinks a coffee with Dona Amélia. At one o'clock he has lunch in the canteen. At a quarter past four he stands under the tower and looks at the clock.

Inês gets up at seven o'clock. Oliver gets up at half past six, because he can't sleep. Tiago gets up at five to eight and arrives at school at twenty-nine minutes past eight. He is very proud of this!

One Wednesday there is fish soup for lunch. Under Oliver's bowl there is a napkin with a message in green ink: "Key number two is in a room with a thousand books. Look for the red dragon." Oliver knows the red dragon. It is on the flag of Wales.

Then Inês looks out of the window, at the tower. The clock moves! There is a man's face in the little window under the clock. He has got a long white beard. But Senhor Bento, Miss Hart and Dona Amélia are all in the canteen. So who is in the tower?

reading.title: The Red Dragon
text: The school library is on the second floor, next to the music room. There are books on the shelves, on the tables and under the chairs. The three friends go there at lunchtime to look for the red dragon.
Every detective in the team has got a talent. Inês can find things. Oliver can read English very fast, and he can draw anything. Tiago can't read fast, but he can climb.
"Have you got a pet, Oliver?" asks Tiago. "I've got a cat in Manchester. She lives with my grandma. Her name is Biscuit." Tiago laughs. Bolacha means biscuit!

On the fourteenth of February, St Valentine's Day, there is a pink card on Tiago's desk: "Roses are red, violets are blue, your dog is lazy, but I love you. Guess who?" The writing is green. "Miss Hart loves me!" says Tiago.

On a rainy Friday, Tiago climbs the ladder. On the top shelf, between a big atlas and a book about cats, there is a red book about Wales. In the middle of the book there is a small golden key and a card: "Key number three is in the capital of Scotland."
Inês puts the two keys in her pencil case. But the next day, after break, the keys aren't there. In their place there is a note in black capital letters: "THE TOWER IS NOT A GAME. STOP NOW."

The UK has got four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Their capitals are London, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast. The King is Charles the Third. One of his homes is Buckingham Palace, in London.
The head teacher has got news: "On the first of June, Children's Day, our school is one hundred years old! I want the old clock to wake up for the party."
At lunchtime, Tiago climbs on a chair and looks behind the big map of the UK, just behind Edinburgh. The third key is there! But who has got keys number one and two?

reading.title: Eggs and Answers
text: It is the last week before the Easter holidays. In the canteen, Tiago always eats everything: soup, rice, chicken, salad and two desserts. Inês never eats fish, and she hardly ever eats salad. Oliver sometimes misses his food from home. "In Manchester I often have beans on toast," he says.

That afternoon there is an Easter egg hunt in the school garden. "In Britain, children often look for chocolate eggs at Easter," says Miss Hart. "We usually eat hot cross buns too." "In Portugal we eat folar and amêndoas," says Inês. "Godparents usually give a folar to their godchildren."

Oliver finds a blue egg with his name on it. Inside there is no chocolate. There is a note: "Don't be angry with the man with the keys. He is a good man. See you at the top of the tower on the first of June, at twelve o'clock. The Fox"

At a quarter past four the friends talk to Senhor Bento. He smiles! "Yes, I've got your keys. The stairs in the tower are very old. A friend of mine is a clockmaker. He repairs the stairs on Wednesdays. In May the stairs are safe, and I give you the keys."
"So you are The Fox!" says Tiago. "No," says Senhor Bento. "The Fox is my big sister."

reading.title: Questions, Questions
text: Who is Senhor Bento's big sister? Inês writes questions in her notebook: Who is she? Where does she live? Why does she write in English?

In May, the class has got a video call with Oliver's old school in Manchester. The English children wear grey jumpers and blue ties. "Why do you wear a uniform?" asks Inês. "Most schools in England have got a uniform," says Amy.

"What do you have for lunch?" asks Tiago. "Some of us have school dinners, and some of us bring a packed lunch from home," says Jack. "Here we've got soup, a main dish and a dessert every day!" says Tiago.
Then Jack asks, "Do you want to come back, Ollie?" Oliver looks at Inês and Tiago. "I don't know," he says.
That evening, Inês walks past the bakery. There is a name on a doorbell. She reads it, and she writes one word in her notebook. "Who is it?" asks Tiago. "Not yet," says Inês.
On the first of June, Senhor Bento gives the friends the keys. "Listen carefully. Open this door with key number one. Go up slowly. Hold the rail. Don't run. Don't touch the old bell."
At the top of the tower, in the clock room, there is a person in a long grey coat. The person has got an orange face, long ears and a black nose. "Hello, detectives," says The Fox. "You're late."

reading.title: Twelve O'Clock
text: The Fox takes off the mask. It is Dona Amélia, the canteen lady! "I'm the soup lady and I'm The Fox," she says. Inês isn't surprised. The name on the doorbell is Amélia Raposo. Raposo, raposa: fox!

In the old photo, Dona Amélia is ten years old and new at the school. Her mother is English and her father is Portuguese. She hasn't got any friends. Then her teacher puts a card with a fox in her desk. With the clues, she finds two best friends.
Oliver's mum is Dona Amélia's friend. They have tea together every Sunday. That's how The Fox knows Oliver's secret. And the green pen? Miss Hart always forgets her pens in the canteen!

It's two minutes to twelve. "Put the key in here. Turn it ten times. Slowly," says Dona Amélia. Oliver, Inês and Tiago turn the key. Click. Tick. Tock. The bell rings twelve times, and two hundred children shout and cheer.
"I don't want a plane ticket now," says Oliver. "Maybe for a visit in August. But then I come back." He wants to buy pastéis de nata for everyone with his forty-two euros.
Dona Amélia gives Inês a new card for September. And the old clock? For the first time in many years, it is right.

sebenta.title: Verb to be
sebenta.html:
Affirmative, negative and question (afirmativa, negativa e interrogativa)

Affirmative (+)Negative (–)Question (?)Short answers
I am (I'm)I am not (I'm not)Am I…?Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
you are (you're)you are not (you aren't)Are you…?Yes, you are. / No, you aren't.
he is (he's)he is not (he isn't)Is he…?Yes, he is. / No, he isn't.
she is (she's)she is not (she isn't)Is she…?Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
it is (it's)it is not (it isn't)Is it…?Yes, it is. / No, it isn't.
we are (we're)we are not (we aren't)Are we…?Yes, we are. / No, we aren't.
you are (you're)you are not (you aren't)Are you…?Yes, you are. / No, you aren't.
they are (they're)they are not (they aren't)Are they…?Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
The short forms (I'm, you're, isn't…) are used when we speak and in informal writing. In short answers we do not use the short form after Yes: Yes, I am. (not Yes, I'm)

When do we use to be?

UseExamples
name and identity (nome)I am Rita. · This is my brother.
age (idade) – not have!I am ten (years old). · She is eleven.
nationality and origin (nacionalidade)We are Portuguese. · He is from London.
jobs (profissões)My mother is a teacher.
description: adjectives (descrição)My dog is big and brown. · They are happy.
place (lugar)The book is on the table. · We are at school.
feelings, the weather and the timeI am hungry. · It is cold. · It is 9 o'clock.

Questions with question words

Question word + am / is / are + subject? What is your name? · How old are you? · Where are you from? · Who is that boy?

Common mistakes: I have 10 years → I am 10. · She hungry → She is hungry. · They is → They are. · Is you happy? → Are you happy?

sebenta.title: Have got
sebenta.html:
Affirmative (+)Negative (–)Question (?)Short answers
I have got (I've got)I have not got (I haven't got)Have I got…?Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
you have got (you've got)you haven't gotHave you got…?Yes, you have. / No, you haven't.
he / she / it has got (he's got)he / she / it has not got (hasn't got)Has he / she / it got…?Yes, he has. / No, he hasn't.
we have got (we've got)we haven't gotHave we got…?Yes, we have. / No, we haven't.
you have got (you've got)you haven't gotHave you got…?Yes, you have. / No, you haven't.
they have got (they've got)they haven't gotHave they got…?Yes, they have. / No, they haven't.
Remember: he, she, it → has got. All the others → have got. She has got a cat. (not She have got)

When do we use have got?

UseExamples
possession – things we own (posse)I've got a new bike. · They've got a big house.
family and pets (família e animais)I've got two sisters. · He hasn't got a dog.
description: hair, eyes, body (descrição física)She's got long hair and blue eyes.
illness (doenças)I've got a headache. · He's got a cold.

Questions

  • Yes / No questions: Have / Has + subject + got…? Have you got a pet? – Yes, I have. · Has she got a brother? – No, she hasn't.
  • Wh- questions: question word + have / has + subject + got? What have you got in your bag? · How many pets has he got?
's can be is or has! She's ten. = She is ten. · She's got a cat. = She has got a cat. Look for got: if you see got, the 's means has.

To be or have got?

to be (ser / estar)have got (ter)
I am 10 years old. (idade)I've got a brother. (família)
She is tall and thin. (adjetivos)She's got brown hair. (partes do corpo)
I am hungry / thirsty / tired / cold.I've got a cold / a headache.

sebenta.title: Pronouns, possessives and possessive case
sebenta.html:
Subject pronoun
(pronome pessoal sujeito)		Possessive determiner
(determinante possessivo)		Examples
I (eu)my (meu, minha)I like my school.
you (tu, você)your (teu, tua)You and your friend.
he (ele)his (dele)He loves his dog.
she (ela)her (dela)She loves her cat.
it (ele / ela – coisas, animais)its (dele / dela)It is a bird. Its wings are blue.
we (nós)our (nosso, nossa)We are in our classroom.
you (vocês)your (vosso, vossa)You are in your classroom.
they (eles, elas)their (deles, delas)They are with their parents.
  • I is always a capital letter (letra maiúscula). You is the same for one person and for many people.
  • He = a boy or a man. She = a girl or a woman. It = a thing, an animal, the weather, the time. Where is my pen? It is on the desk.
  • The possessive determiner depends on the owner (dono), not on the thing: Tom and his sister (dele) · Ana and her brother (dela).
  • Possessives always come before a noun and never change: my book · my books (not mys).
its ≠ it's: its = dele/dela (The dog is in its bed); it's = it is (It's a big dog). · his ≠ he's: his = dele; he's = he is.

Possessive case: 's (caso possessivo)

To say who something belongs to, we add 's to the name of the owner. The owner comes first, then the thing: Rita's bag = a mala da Rita (not the bag of Rita).

RuleExamples
one owner (singular) → name + 'smy father's car · Tom's dog · the teacher's desk
names ending in -s → 'sLuís's pencil · Carlos's house
plural owners ending in -s → only 'my parents' room · the girls' toilets
irregular plurals (children, men, women) → 'sthe children's playground
two owners → 's on the last nameAna and Rui's grandmother

We use 's for people and animals. For things, we use of: the door of the classroom · the name of the street.

Whose…? (de quem?) asks about the owner: Whose pen is this? – It's Maria's. / It's her pen.

sebenta.title: Articles and plural of nouns
sebenta.html:
Indefinite article: a / an (um, uma)

RuleExamples
a + consonant sound (som de consoante)a book · a dog · a teacher · a yellow pen
an + vowel sound: a, e, i, o, u (som de vogal)an apple · an egg · an ice cream · an orange · an umbrella
Careful! It is the sound, not the lettera university, a uniform (sound /ju:/) · an hour (h is silent)
  • A / an is used only with singular nouns: a cat but cats (not a cats).
  • Use a / an for jobs: My aunt is a doctor. · He is an actor.

Definite article: the (o, a, os, as)

The is the same for singular and plural, masculine and feminine: the boy · the girls · the books. We use the when we know which one: I've got a dog and a cat. The dog is black. Also: the sun, the moon, the sea (there is only one).

No article (sem artigo) with: meals (I have lunch at one), school subjects (I like Maths), sports (We play football), languages and countries (English, Portugal), and general plurals (Dogs are friendly).

Plural of nouns (plural dos nomes)

RuleExamples
most nouns: + -sbook → books · cat → cats · pen → pens · girl → girls
nouns ending in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: + -esbus → buses · class → classes · dish → dishes · watch → watches · box → boxes · tomato → tomatoes
consonant + -y: -y → -iesbaby → babies · family → families · city → cities
vowel + -y: just + -sboy → boys · day → days · key → keys · toy → toys
nouns ending in -f / -fe: → -vesleaf → leaves · wolf → wolves · knife → knives · life → lives
irregular plurals (learn them by heart!)man → men · woman → women · child → children · person → people · foot → feet · tooth → teeth · mouse → mice
same form in singular and pluralone sheep → two sheep · one fish → two fish

Exceptions: photo → photos, piano → pianos, roof → roofs.

Plural nouns do not use a / an and use are: The children are in the garden. (not The childrens is). Pronunciation of -s: /s/ after p, t, k, f (cats, books); /z/ after vowels and other sounds (dogs, pens); /ɪz/ after -es (buses, boxes).

sebenta.title: There is / there are
sebenta.html:
SingularPluralExamples
+There is (There's) + a / an / oneThere are + two, some, a lot ofThere is a bed in my room. · There are two chairs.
–There isn't + a / anThere aren't + anyThere isn't a TV. · There aren't any plants.
?Is there + a / an…?Are there + any…?Is there a garden? · Are there any posters?
short answersYes, there is. / No, there isn't.Yes, there are. / No, there aren't.Is there a lamp? – Yes, there is.
  • There is + singular noun; there are + plural noun. Look at the first noun: There is a sofa and two armchairs. · There are two armchairs and a sofa.
  • Some (+) in affirmative sentences; any (–, ?) in negatives and questions: There are some books. · There aren't any books. · Are there any books?
  • How many…? (quantos?): How many rooms are there in your house? – There are five.
  • We often use there is / are to describe a house, a room, a school or a town: In my bedroom there is a desk and there are lots of books.
Do not confuse there (há) with their (deles) and they're (they are): There is a dog. · It's their dog. · They're happy. Also: There is ≠ It is: There is a cat on the sofa. It is black.

7Demonstratives (este, esse, aquele)

Near (perto)Far (longe)
Singularthis (este, esta, isto)
This is my pencil. · This book is new.		that (esse, aquele, aquilo)
That is my school. · That boy is my cousin.
Pluralthese (estes, estas)
These are my pencils. · These books are new.		those (esses, aqueles)
Those are my friends. · Those boys are my cousins.
  • Demonstratives can come alone (This is nice.) or before a noun (This T-shirt is nice.).
  • Questions: What's this? – It's a ruler. · What are those? – They're erasers. Answer with it / they.
  • Introducing people: This is my friend Pedro. · These are my parents.
  • On the phone: Hello, this is Ana. · With time: this morning, this week, this year.
Pronunciation: this /ðɪs/ has a short i; these /ðiːz/ has a long ee. Listen to the end: this → /s/, these → /z/.

sebenta.title: Prepositions of place and time
sebenta.html:
Prepositions of place (preposições de lugar) – Where is it?

PrepositionMeaningExamples
indentro de, emThe pen is in the pencil case. · I live in Lisbon.
onem cima de (tocando)The book is on the desk. · The picture is on the wall.
underdebaixo deThe cat is under the bed.
behindatrás deThe ball is behind the door.
in front ofà frente deThe teacher is in front of the board.
next to / besideao lado deThe lamp is next to the bed.
betweenentre (dois)The table is between the chairs.
nearperto deMy school is near my house.
oppositeem frente a (do outro lado)The bank is opposite the park.
above / belowpor cima de / por baixo de (sem tocar)The clock is above the door.
atem (num ponto, lugar)I'm at school. · She's at home. · at the bus stop
in / on / at for places: in a room, a box, a city, a country (in the kitchen, in Porto) · on a surface, a floor, a street (on the floor, on the first floor) · at a point or a place with an activity (at school, at the cinema, at the door).

Prepositions of time (preposições de tempo) – When?

PrepositionUseExamples
athours · night · the weekend · festivalsat 8 o'clock · at half past two · at night · at the weekend · at Christmas · at lunchtime
ondays of the week · dates · day + part of the dayon Monday · on Mondays · on 5th March · on my birthday · on Friday morning
inmonths · seasons · years · parts of the dayin June · in summer · in 2026 · in the morning / afternoon / evening
from … tostart and endSchool is from 8.30 to 1.30.
before / afterantes de / depois debefore dinner · after school
Remember the "triangle": at = exact time (at 9) · on = day (on Sunday) · in = longer period (in May, in winter). But: in the morning / at night / on Sunday morning. No preposition with today, tomorrow, every day, this week.

sebenta.title: Can
sebenta.html:
Affirmative (+)Negative (–)Question (?)Short answers
I / you / he / she / it / we / they can + verbI / you / he / she / it / we / they cannot (can't) + verbCan I / you / he… + verb?Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
I can swim.
She can play the piano.		I can't fly.
He can't cook.		Can you dance?
Can birds talk?		Yes, I can.
No, they can't.
  • Can is the same for all persons: she can (not she cans). The verb after can has no to and no -s: He can run (not can to run, can runs).
  • Questions and negatives are made without do: Can you swim? (not Do you can swim?)
UseExamples
ability (capacidade – saber fazer)I can speak English. · My baby brother can't walk. · Elephants can't jump.
permission (permissão – poder)Can I go to the toilet, please? · You can't use your phone in class.
requests (pedidos)Can you help me, please? · Can you repeat that, please?
possibility (possibilidade)We can go to the beach at the weekend.
Asking about ability: What can you do? – I can sing and dance. · How well can you swim? – Very well. / Quite well. / Not very well. With very / quite / really well after the verb: She can play tennis very well.

10Imperative (imperativo – ordens e instruções)

FormExamplesUse
Affirmative:
verb (base form)		Open your books. · Sit down. · Listen to the teacher. · Turn left.orders, instructions, directions (ordens, instruções, direções)
Negative:
Don't + verb		Don't run in the corridor. · Don't talk! · Don't be late.prohibitions and warnings (proibições e avisos)
Let's + verb
Let's not + verb		Let's play football! · Let's go home. · Let's not be late.suggestions – you and me (sugestões: vamos…)
  • The imperative has no subject: we don't say You open the door, we say Open the door.
  • Add please to be polite: Please close the window. / Close the window, please.
  • The imperative of be is Be / Don't be: Be quiet! · Don't be sad.
Classroom instructions: Open / Close your books · Listen · Repeat · Look at the board · Read the text · Write the answers · Work in pairs · Stand up / Sit down · Put up your hand · Be quiet · Don't shout · Come here · Hurry up!

sebenta.title: Present simple (1)
sebenta.html:
We use the present simple for habits and routines (hábitos e rotinas), things that are always true (factos), and likes and dislikes (gostos): I get up at 7. · The sun rises in the east. · She likes pizza.

Affirmative (+)

I / you / we / they + verbhe / she / it + verb + -s
I play football. · We live in Porto. · They like pizza.He plays football. · She lives in Porto. · My cat likes fish.

Spelling of the 3rd person (he / she / it)

RuleExamples
most verbs: + -swork → works · play → plays · read → reads · eat → eats
verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: + -eswash → washes · watch → watches · go → goes · do → does · fix → fixes
consonant + -y: -y → -iesstudy → studies · fly → flies · carry → carries (but play → plays)
irregularhave → has · be → is

Negative (–): don't / doesn't + verb

I / you / we / they + don't + verbhe / she / it + doesn't + verb
I don't like cheese. · They don't live here.He doesn't like cheese. · She doesn't live here.
After doesn't the verb has no -s: She doesn't play (not She doesn't plays). don't = do not · doesn't = does not.

Questions (?): Do / Does + subject + verb?

Do + I / you / we / they + verb?Does + he / she / it + verb?
Do you like music? – Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
Do they go to school by bus? – Yes, they do.		Does she like music? – Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
Does he go to school by bus? – No, he doesn't.

Wh- questions: question word + do / does + subject + verb? What time do you get up? · Where does she live? · What does he do after school?

Daily routine verbs (rotina diária)

get up · have a shower · get dressed · have breakfast · brush my teeth · go to school · have lunch · have classes · come home · do my homework · play with my friends · watch TV · have dinner · go to bed

sebenta.title: Present simple (2): adverbs of frequency
sebenta.html:
AdverbHow often?Examples
alwayssempre · 100%I always brush my teeth.
usuallynormalmente · 80%She usually walks to school.
oftenmuitas vezes · 60%We often play in the park.
sometimesàs vezes · 40%They sometimes eat pizza.
rarely / hardly everraramente · 10%He rarely watches TV.
nevernunca · 0%I never drink coffee.
  • Position: before the main verb (I always get up at 7.) but after the verb to be (I am always happy. · He is never late.).
  • With never the verb is affirmative: I never eat meat. (not I don't never eat)
  • Other expressions (at the end of the sentence): every day / week / Monday · once a week · twice a month · three times a year · on Saturdays · at the weekend. I have English twice a week.
How often…? (com que frequência?) How often do you play football? – Twice a week. / Every day. / I never play football.
